en: Open your medicine box and pull one capsule apart. Any antibiotic will do.
See that white powder inside? That powder is the medicine. Everything else is just packing.
Now keep that powder in mind... and come with me to the third of March, twenty twenty.

Delhi. A one-page government order goes out, and if you run a medicine company, your phone starts ringing. Twenty-six medicine ingredients can't leave India without a licence. Paracetamol is one of them.
Wait. India? The country the whole world calls the pharmacy of the world... locking its own doors?
Yes. And the reason was far away. A province in China called Hubei had just shut down for the virus.
About half the ingredients on that list came mainly from that one province.
So here's the question I want to answer for you today. If India makes medicine for the world... who makes the powder inside India's medicine?
The answer may make you a little uneasy. But stay with me. Around minute nine, I'll show you a fight India is winning right now — in Andhra Pradesh — and the exact date it gets decided.
First, let's give India its due. Because that pharmacy of the world title? India earned it.
Think back to two thousand one. H.I.V. is killing millions in Africa. The medicines exist... but the Western price is around ten thousand dollars a year for one patient.
Then an Indian company, Cipla, stands up and offers the same three-drug cocktail for about a dollar a day.
One dollar. That one offer helped change how the world priced these medicines.
And today? Indian medicines go to around two hundred countries. Count the pills, and you'll find India is the third biggest maker of medicines in the world.
Last year India exported medicines worth about thirty billion dollars. That's more than two and a half lakh crore rupees.
So where's the missing piece? Here's the catch. Every tablet has two parts.
There's the powder that actually makes you better. Doctors call it the A.P.I., the active pharmaceutical ingredient. Let's just call it the powder.
And then there's everything around it... the rest of the tablet, the coating, the strip, the box.
And you should know this — Indian companies are world class at the last part. Mixing, pressing, packing, and passing the toughest inspections on the planet.
But the powder you swallow? A lot of it is made somewhere else first.
In twenty twenty-five, India bought about seven point four billion dollars of these powders from other countries. By our maths, that's around sixty-five thousand crore rupees.
And the biggest seller, by far... China.
And if you look at antibiotics, it gets worse. According to Niti Aayog, out of every hundred rupees India spent on imported antibiotic ingredients... about eighty-six went to China.

Even your fever tablet has a China link. Indian factories do make paracetamol powder. But one step earlier, there's a chemical called para-aminophenol... and industry reports say a big share of that still comes from China.
So you might be thinking — has it always been like this? Did India ever make its own powder?
It did. And this part of the story, most people have never heard.
Pimpri, near Pune. Nineteen fifty-four. India has been free for barely seven years, and it decides to make its own penicillin.
Penicillin was the miracle drug of that time. Imagine you got a small cut that could kill you... and now it was just a few days of medicine.
The government sets up a company called Hindustan Antibiotics. By nineteen fifty-six, Indian penicillin is coming out of Indian tanks.
Think about that, would you? A young, poor country, growing one of the most important medicines on earth... on its own.
And over the next decades, more companies join in. Alembic, Sarabhai, Ranbaxy, Torrent, and the state-owned I.D.P.L.
So how do you actually make penicillin? This is the part that decides everything, so let me show you.
You see, paracetamol is cooked from chemicals, step by step. Penicillin is different. Penicillin is grown.
You take a special mould... a cousin of the green patches you've seen on old bread. You put it in a giant steel tank, and you feed it sugar and air.
For about a week, the tank runs day and night. The mould eats, grows, and pours out penicillin into the liquid.
Then you pull the penicillin out, and you clean it. That's called penicillin G.
Next, an enzyme cuts it into a smaller base, called six A.P.A. And from that base, you build the antibiotics you actually take — like amoxicillin.
Now here's the secret of this business. A bigger tank makes the powder cheaper. Much cheaper.
Why? The tank must stay perfectly clean, cool, and full of air, every hour of every day. That takes a lot of power, water and steam.
Double your tank, and your bill doesn't double. But your output does. And if one tiny bug gets in, you can lose the whole batch.
So the country with the biggest tanks and the cheapest power... wins. Simple as that.
And that's exactly where India's story turns.
For years, India's government licensed only a few companies to make penicillin, and only in small amounts. Researchers say the plants stayed too small to be cheap.
Meanwhile, in the nineteen nineties, China decided medicine ingredients were a strategic industry.
It built huge plants, in huge chemical parks, with cheap power and cheap water. Its factories also faced looser pollution rules.
And then Chinese penicillin flooded the world market... at prices nobody else could match.
Now look at this number, and hold on to it. In nineteen ninety-one, China's share of India's medicine ingredient imports was less than one per cent.
Less than one.
Then, one by one, the Indian penicillin plants went quiet.
Hindustan Antibiotics. Stopped.
Alembic. Sarabhai. Stopped.
I.D.P.L. Torrent. Ranbaxy. Stopped.
By the end of the twenty tens, India was importing all of its six A.P.A. — the base for amoxicillin. Every last kilo.
And that one per cent? Today, it's around eighty-six per cent for antibiotics.
Niti Aayog says Chinese ingredients cost thirty-five to forty per cent less than ones made in India. So tell me — if you ran a company, would you build a plant here?
That's the trap. You can't compete without a big plant. And you can't risk a big plant... when one price war can wipe it out.
For thirty years, that trap held. Then twenty twenty happened — the locked doors I showed you at the start.
And this time, Delhi decided to break it.
The government launched a scheme. It would pay companies an incentive to make forty-one of these missing ingredients in India, with nearly seven thousand crore rupees set aside.
And one company took the biggest bet of all.
Kakinada, Andhra Pradesh. On the coast, a new plant goes up, built by Aurobindo Pharma's unit, Lyfius.
Inside are the giant tanks we just talked about. Built to make fifteen thousand tonnes of penicillin G a year, at a cost of around two and a half thousand crore rupees.
In twenty twenty-four, the tanks start running. For the first time in about thirty years... India is growing its own penicillin again.
But you know the trap. As soon as Indian penicillin arrived, cheap imports were still waiting at the port.
So on the twenty-ninth of January, twenty twenty-six, the government did something it rarely does.
It set a floor price. Penicillin G cannot come into India below about two thousand two hundred rupees a kilo. Amoxicillin and six A.P.A. got floors too.
Think of it as a shield. It gives the new Indian plant breathing room, while it grows big enough to stand on its own.
But that shield has an end date. It runs for one year... until January twenty twenty-seven.
That's the date to watch. Is Kakinada strong enough by then, do you think? Or does the shield get extended?
And it's not just penicillin. By June twenty twenty-six, companies under the scheme had put in more than five thousand crore rupees, for twenty-eight ingredients.
Three giant bulk drug parks are coming up too... in Gujarat, Himachal Pradesh, and at Nakkapalli in Andhra Pradesh.
Let me be honest with you. Most of those parks aren't running yet. And China has a thirty-year head start, with tanks far bigger than ours.
So here's the rule I take from all this. If you only master the last step, you're only as strong as whoever controls the step before.
And the cost? You saw it in twenty twenty. When one province shut down, the pharmacy of the world had to lock its own doors.
But here's the reality today. India has the scientists. It has the doctors and the factories. And now, for the first time in decades, it's growing its own penicillin again.
So what does this mean for you?
Your medicines are safe, and you don't need to change anything you buy. This isn't about quality. It's about who holds the switch.
The next time you take an antibiotic, think about that white powder. There's a fair chance part of its journey began in China.
But if Kakinada wins... the next one might start in Andhra.
And medicines aren't the only missing piece. India writes software for the whole world. So why doesn't it have its own giant A.I.? That's our next story.
Before you go, tell me in the comments — which medicine in your home would you most like to see fully made in India? I read every one.
